concept.name: CAP Theorem & PACELC

reviewRecord.reviewNotes: Seeded for SPEC-062 pillar coverage matrix.

spark.summary: CAP proves a distributed data store cannot simultaneously guarantee linearizability (C) and 100% availability (A) during a network partition (P); PACELC extends this to normal operation, forcing a choice between latency (L) and consistency (C) even when no partition exists.
spark.keyTakeaway: Because network partitions are inevitable, the real-world design choice is not 'CP vs AP'—it is whether you pay the cross-region latency tax on every write during healthy operation (PC/EC) or accept stale reads and conflict resolution (PA/EL).

concept.whyItMatters: Treating 'CAP' as a binary label leads engineers to pick eventual consistency when they actually need linearizable uniqueness (like inventory or bank balances), or to deploy synchronous multi-region Raft and wonder why every write takes 85ms. Understanding PACELC and the consistency hierarchy lets you match exact protocol guarantees to each business invariant.
whenToUse: Choose CP / PC-EC (Raft, Paxos, Spanner, etcd, CockroachDB) for distributed locks, leader election, financial ledgers, and unique-constraint enforcement where stale reads or split-brain writes corrupt data.

Choose AP / PA-EL (Dynamo-style `W=1, R=1`, Cassandra with `LOCAL_ONE`, CRDTs) for shopping carts, user activity feeds, metrics, and edge caches where sub-10ms local writes and partition survival outweigh immediate global consistency.
Use tunable per-operation consistency (e.g., Cassandra `LOCAL_QUORUM` for profile updates vs `LOCAL_ONE` for view counters) to avoid paying global coordination costs uniformly.
whenNotToUse: Avoid strong global consensus (PC/EC across continents) on high-throughput user-facing writes if your p99 latency budget is <30ms—physics sets cross-ocean RTT at ~75–150ms.
Avoid AP eventual consistency for strict invariants (account balances, seat reservations, distributed mutexes) where concurrent writes cannot be safely merged post-hoc.
Avoid applying CAP to single-node databases or single-AZ synchronous primary-standby setups without understanding that a single-node DB is neither partition-tolerant nor highly available.
keyPoints: CAP's 'C' specifically means **Linearizability** (every read sees the latest completed write in real-time order), and 'A' means every non-failing node must respond—a strict definition violated if a minority partition refuses writes.
PACELC (Daniel Abadi, 2012) captures the missing half: **if P** (partition), choose **A or C**; **else (E)** (normal operation), choose **L (latency) or C (consistency)**.

Quorum math ($W + R > N$) provides overlap in a 3-node replica set ($N=3, W=2, R=2$), but does **not** automatically guarantee linearizability without read-repair or leader-based ordering (e.g., Raft).

Consistency models form a strict spectrum from strongest to weakest: **Linearizable** -> **Sequential** -> **Causal** (preserves happens-before, e.g., comments after posts) -> **Read-Your-Writes** -> **Eventual**.
Jepsen testing repeatedly proved that misconfigured 'CP' databases (e.g., clock-skew bugs, dirty reads, unpinned leaders) silently lose linearizability under asymmetric partitions.

examples.title: CockroachDB / Spanner (PC/EC) vs. DynamoDB Global Tables (PA/EL)
examples.scenario: A global fintech ledger deploys across US-East, EU-West, and AP-South (~80ms inter-region RTT). CockroachDB uses Raft consensus requiring a majority quorum (2 of 3 regions) per write; DynamoDB Global Tables accepts writes locally in <10ms and replicates asynchronously.
examples.outcome: CockroachDB guarantees linearizable balances with zero lost commits during a region split, at an ~80ms write latency floor. DynamoDB sustains 8ms local writes during partitions, but concurrent updates to the same key in two regions trigger Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.

examples.title: PostgreSQL `synchronous_commit` Tuning Across Availability Zones
examples.scenario: A primary PostgreSQL instance in `us-east-1a` replicates to a standby in `us-east-1b` (0.8ms RTT). With `synchronous_commit = on`, the primary waits for the standby to flush WAL to disk before acknowledging `COMMIT`.
examples.outcome: If the AZ link partitions, writes block until failover (CP / PC-EC), guaranteeing zero data loss (RPO=0) at a +0.8ms write latency cost. Switching to `synchronous_commit = local` drops latency by 0.8ms (PA/EL) but risks losing the last few milliseconds of committed transactions on primary crash.

tradeOffs.factor: Linearizability vs. Tail Latency (EC vs. EL)
tradeOffs.pro: Synchronous quorum replication guarantees every client sees the exact same latest state with zero conflict-resolution code.
tradeOffs.con: Write latency is bounded by the slowest node in the quorum (e.g., 75ms+ cross-region), and a partition stalls the minority side.

tradeOffs.factor: Availability Under Partitions vs. Anomaly Risk
tradeOffs.pro: AP/EL systems accept writes on both sides of a split, keeping checkout carts or telemetry ingestion at 99.999% uptime.
tradeOffs.con: Divergent writes require deterministic merge logic (CRDTs, vector clocks, or LWW), and LWW silently drops concurrent updates.

tradeOffs.factor: Causal Consistency as the Sweet Spot
tradeOffs.pro: Available under partitions (no global consensus needed) while preventing impossible timelines like seeing a reply before its parent post.
tradeOffs.con: Requires tracking causal metadata (Lamport/hybrid logical clocks or session tokens) across every read and write.

failureModes.name: Sloppy Quorum + Last-Write-Wins Silent Data Loss
failureModes.description: In an AP store using wall-clock timestamps (`LWW`), a node with 200ms NTP clock drift silently overwrites newer writes from other nodes without raising an error.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC), CRDTs (G-Counter, OR-Set), or strict quorum (`W + R > N` with Raft/Paxos) instead of raw wall-clock LWW.

failureModes.name: Asymmetric Network Partition Causes Dual Leaders
failureModes.description: Node A can reach B, B can reach C, but A cannot reach C. Without strict term/lease fencing, both A and C believe they are the primary and accept conflicting writes.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Raft/Paxos term numbers plus fencing tokens on storage/locks, and validate with Jepsen fault injection.

failureModes.name: Stale Reads from Follower Without Read-Index
failureModes.description: Serving reads from a Raft follower without checking the leader's `commitIndex` returns stale data even in a CP cluster, breaking linearizability.
failureModes.mitigation: Route linearizable reads through the leader (with `ReadIndex` or leader leases bounded by clock-skew uncertainty).

failureModes.name: Read-Your-Writes Violation After Load-Balanced Write
failureModes.description: A user updates their profile on primary, then immediately refreshes and hits an async read replica 150ms behind, seeing their old profile and retrying.
failureModes.mitigation: Pin the user's session to primary for 1–2 seconds post-write or pass a causal LSN/timestamp token so replicas wait until caught up.

commonMistakes: Calling a system 'CA'—in any networked distributed system, partitions (P) happen, so 'CA' only describes a single-node database or an impossible ideal.
Assuming `W + R > N` in a leaderless Dynamo store guarantees linearizability (concurrent writes without read-repair or consensus can still return stale values).
Using `Last-Write-Wins` with unsynchronized NTP clocks (10–100ms drift) for financial or inventory mutations.
Enabling multi-region synchronous consensus when only 5% of tables (e.g., billing) need linearizability and 95% (e.g., logs/preferences) can be local.
Confusing ACID isolation levels (Serializable) with distributed consistency (Linearizability)—a database can be Serializable on stale snapshots.

sections.content:
## The idea

Eric Brewer's **CAP Theorem** (formalized by Gilbert & Lynch, 2002) proves that when a network partition (**P**) splits a distributed store into disconnected groups of nodes, the system must choose between **Consistency** (linearizability: every read returns the most recent write or an error) and **Availability** (every non-failing node returns a non-error response, even if stale). Because partitions are unavoidable in real networks, **PACELC** (Abadi, 2012) completes the picture: during a partition (**P**), choose **A or C**; else (**E**, normal operation), choose between **Latency (L)** and **Consistency (C)**.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a 3-node key-value cluster (`N1` in US-East, `N2` in US-Central, `N3` in US-West) holding `balance = $100`:

1. **Healthy Operation (Else branch of PACELC)**:
   - **PC/EC (e.g., etcd / CockroachDB Raft)**: `N1` (leader) receives `SET balance = $80`, replicates to `N2` (25ms RTT), reaches quorum (2/3), and acknowledges. Every subsequent read sees `$80`, paying a +25ms latency cost.
   - **PA/EL (e.g., Cassandra `LOCAL_ONE`)**: `N1` writes locally in 1ms and acknowledges immediately, replicating to `N2`/`N3` asynchronously.
2. **During a Partition (`N1` isolated from `N2, N3`)**:
   - **CP**: `N1` cannot reach a majority quorum (1 < 2), so it **refuses writes** (sacrificing A) while `N2, N3` elect a new leader and remain consistent.
   - **AP**: `N1` continues accepting `SET balance = $60` while `N2` accepts `SET balance = $50`, creating divergent state that must be reconciled once the partition heals.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / The consistency spectrum beyond binary CAP
sections.content:
## The consistency spectrum beyond binary CAP

Real systems rarely sit at only two extremes; they form a hierarchy of guarantees:
1. **Linearizability (Strict/External Consistency)**: Single-copy illusion ordered by real-time wall clock (etcd, Google Spanner via TrueTime `[-7ms, +7ms]`).
2. **Sequential Consistency**: All nodes see operations in the same total order, though not necessarily matching real-time order across independent clients.
3. **Causal Consistency**: Operations that are causally related (`A -> B`) appear in order everywhere; concurrent unrelated operations may appear in different orders.
4. **Session Guarantees (Read-Your-Writes / Monotonic Reads)**: A single user always sees their own updates and never moves backward in time.
5. **Eventual Consistency**: If writes stop, all replicas eventually converge to the same state.

## PACELC classification of real-world databases

| System | PACELC Class | Replication Protocol | Typical Write Latency | Conflict / Partition Behavior |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **etcd / ZooKeeper** | PC / EC | Raft / ZAB | 2–10ms (intra-region) | Minority partition rejects all writes |
| **CockroachDB / Spanner** | PC / EC | Multi-Raft / Paxos + HLC/TrueTime | 20–85ms (cross-region) | Linearizable; minority stalls until healed |
| **DynamoDB (Eventual) / Cassandra (`ONE`)** | PA / EL | Leaderless / Async Global | 1–10ms (local AZ) | High availability; LWW or CRDT merge |
| **MongoDB (default `w:majority`)** | PC / EC | Primary-Secondary Raft-like | 2–25ms | Minority primary steps down on partition |
| **PostgreSQL (Async Replica)** | PA / EL (if promoted) | WAL streaming | <1ms local commit | Risk of RPO > 0 and split-brain without fencing |

## Failure modes

1. **Clock-Skew Silent Overwrites**: Using `LWW` when NTP drifts by 150ms causes older writes from a fast-clock node to overwrite newer writes from a slow-clock node.
2. **Split-Brain Promotion**: Manually promoting an async read replica during a transient network blip while the old primary still accepts writes creates two divergent histories.
3. **Gray Failures / Asymmetric Partitions**: Node A cannot reach Node B, but both reach clients; naive health checks pass while quorum heartbeats flap continuously.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Mixing consistency models in one architecture
sections.content:
## Mixing consistency models in one architecture

Production architectures rarely apply one PACELC choice globally. Place **identity, billing, inventory reservation, and leader election** on a PC/EC store (PostgreSQL/Spanner/etcd) where correctness trumps a 10–50ms write tax. Place **shopping carts, session caches, user feeds, and telemetry** on PA/EL or causal stores (Redis, DynamoDB, Cassandra) using idempotent updates or CRDTs so local reads and writes stay under 5ms even during cross-AZ or cross-region degradation.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Map every data entity to its required invariant: Linearizable (money/locks), Causal (social/comments), or Eventual (counters/caches).
- [ ] For PC/EC stores, size quorum placement across 3 failure domains (AZs or regions) and measure exact inter-zone RTT.
- [ ] For PA/EL stores, replace raw wall-clock `LWW` with Hybrid Logical Clocks, CRDTs, or explicit conflict-resolution handlers.
- [ ] Configure fencing tokens (`STONITH` / Raft term IDs) on primary-standby databases to prevent split-brain on failover.
- [ ] Implement Read-Your-Writes session stickiness or LSN-wait when serving reads from asynchronous replicas.

interviewProblems.title: CAP Theorem & Consistency Models
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on CAP Theorem & Consistency Models. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Cap Theorem Consistency Models

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: CAP proves a distributed data store cannot simultaneously guarantee linearizability (C) and 100% availability (A) during a network partition (P); PACELC extends this to normal operation, forcing a choice between latency (L) and consistency (C) even when no partition exists.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Nodes N2 & N3 applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Protocol Decision.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Protocol Decision experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC), CRDTs (G-Counter, OR-Set), or strict quorum (`W + R > N` with Raft/Paxos) instead of raw wall-clock LWW.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Because network partitions are inevitable, the real-world design choice is not 'CP vs AP'—it is whether you pay the cross-region latency tax on every write during healthy operation (PC/EC) or accept stale reads and conflict resolution (PA/EL).
Avoid trap: Calling a system 'CA'—in any networked distributed system, partitions (P) happen, so 'CA' only describes a single-node database or an impossible ideal.
Avoid trap: Assuming `W + R > N` in a leaderless Dynamo store guarantees linearizability (concurrent writes without read-repair or consensus can still return stale values).

When to reach for it: Choose CP / PC-EC (Raft, Paxos, Spanner, etcd, CockroachDB) for distributed locks, leader election, financial ledgers, and unique-constraint enforcement where stale reads or split-brain writes corrupt data.

When to reach for it: Choose AP / PA-EL (Dynamo-style `W=1, R=1`, Cassandra with `LOCAL_ONE`, CRDTs) for shopping carts, user activity feeds, metrics, and edge caches where sub-10ms local writes and partition survival outweigh immediate global consistency.

putItTogether.title: Putting Cap Theorem Consistency Models Together
putItTogether.summary: Because network partitions are inevitable, the real-world design choice is not 'CP vs AP'—it is whether you pay the cross-region latency tax on every write during healthy operation (PC/EC) or accept stale reads and conflict resolution (PA/EL).
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Cap Theorem Consistency Models before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: CockroachDB guarantees linearizable balances with zero lost commits during a region split, at an ~80ms write latency floor. DynamoDB sustains 8ms local writes during partitions, but concurrent updates to the same key in two regions trigger Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
